hints: Think about the journey of the radiation from inside the nucleus to inside the detector - what could stop it or block it on the way?
Think about counts that the detector records that do not come from this source at all, and also about times when the detector misses a decay because it is busy or insensitive.
walkthrough:
**Separate Activity From Count Rate**
Activity $A$ is the true number of decays per second in the source. Count rate is what your detector actually clicks. They are never equal because not every decay produces a click, and not every click comes from the source.

**Reasons For Fewer Counts Than Decays**
Some radiation is absorbed in the source itself (self-absorption), in the air, or in the window of the detector before it can ionise the gas inside. Also the detector may be insensitive to some radiations, and it has a dead-time after each count when it cannot record the next decay.

**Reasons For Extra Counts**
The detector also records background radiation from cosmic rays, rocks, and other sources nearby. Daughter products formed in the source may also emit extra radiation.

Final answer: Any two from: background radiation increases measured rate; absorption in air / self-absorption in source / absorption in detector window reduces measured rate; detector does not detect all types of radiation; detector dead-time misses counts.

hints: Look very closely at the thickness and smoothness of the line in Fig. 12.1 - if decay were perfectly predictable, what shape would you expect?
walkthrough:
**Link Random To Graph Shape**
Random means you cannot predict exactly when a particular nucleus will decay, so the count in any one minute jumps up and down statistically. On a graph this appears as small rapid wiggles or jaggedness on top of the smooth exponential fall, exactly as seen in Fig. 12.1.
Final answer: The plotted curve is not smooth / is jagged and fluctuates up and down, showing random variation in count rate.

hints: Look at the far right of the graph where the curve has flattened out - what steady value does it tend to, and why must this be removed first?
After subtracting that steady value, pick a clear starting corrected count rate on the smooth trend and halve it to find the time for one half-life.
To improve reliability, repeat the halving process starting from a different time - for example halve again to a quarter of the original.
Check that your two or three values for the time interval agree to about 1.5 hours and consider drawing a smooth best-fit line through the wiggles to read more accurately.
walkthrough:
**Correct For Background**
At large $t$, e.g. $t = 10$ to $14\text{ h}$, the count rate levels off at about $10\text{ min}^{-1}$. This is background, not from the source. So true source rate = measured rate $- 10\text{ min}^{-1}$. Forgetting this is the most common mistake.

**Find First Half-Life**
Take the smooth trend through the wiggles. At $t = 0$, measured $\approx 170\text{ min}^{-1}$, so corrected $A_0 \approx 160\text{ min}^{-1}$. Half is $80\text{ min}^{-1}$ corrected, i.e. $90\text{ min}^{-1}$ measured. From the graph this occurs at $$t \approx 1.5\text{ h}$$

**Repeat To Confirm**
Halve again: $40\text{ min}^{-1}$ corrected is $50\text{ min}^{-1}$ measured, occurring at $t \approx 3.0\text{ h}$. The interval $3.0 - 1.5 = 1.5\text{ h}$ confirms the result. Averaging two determinations reduces error from randomness.

**State Result**
Both intervals give $$T_{1/2} \approx 1.4 \text{ to } 1.6\text{ h, about } 1.5\text{ h}$$ This is the half-life of the isotope, independent of detector efficiency.

Final answer: Background $\approx 10\text{ min}^{-1}$ subtracted. Corrected initial rate $\approx 160\text{ min}^{-1}$ falls to $80\text{ min}^{-1}$ in $\approx 1.5\text{ h}$, to $40\text{ min}^{-1}$ in a further $\approx 1.5\text{ h}$. Half-life $\approx 1.5\text{ hours}$.

hints: Recall whether radioactive decay is controlled by the nucleus alone or by outside conditions like heat, pressure or chemical state.
If the outside condition cannot change the decay probability, what does that tell you about the half-life of the heated sample?
Even with the same half-life and same starting rate, will the exact clicks at a later time be identical - think back to part (b)(i)?
walkthrough:
**Half-Life Is Fixed By The Nucleus**
Decay constant $\lambda$ depends only on nuclear stability, not on thermal motion of atoms. Heating to $500^{\circ}\text{C}$ changes electron energies by a fraction of an eV, while nuclear energies are in MeV. So the probability of decay per second is unchanged.

**No Change In Half-Life**
Since $$T_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda}$$ and $\lambda$ is unchanged, $T_{1/2}$ is unchanged. The decay curve falls at the same average rate.

**Count Rate Still Varies Randomly**
The measured count at any specific $t$ is a random sample around the expected exponential value. Two repeats will almost never give exactly the same number, so the heated run could show a slightly different count rate even though the underlying half-life is identical.

Final answer: 1. Half-life: no change, because radioactive decay is spontaneous and unaffected by temperature / external environment. 2. Measured count rate at a given time: may be slightly different because decay and counting are random processes.
